exercises.title: Explaining what an Architecture Decision Record actually is
exercises.situation: A product manager notices engineers keep referencing "ADR-014" in Slack instead of just telling her the decision directly, and asks what an ADR actually is and why the team bothers with it instead of just deciding things in a meeting.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's just a doc where we write down what we decided, so people don't have to keep asking about it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It never explains the actual problem an ADR solves — that a decision made only in a meeting lives in people's memory and gets lost, misremembered, or re-litigated. It also skips the specific structure (context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered) and never explains why the rejected alternatives are often the most valuable part, which is the detail a PM would actually find useful the next time she's told "we already looked at that."
exercises.professionalResponse: An ADR is a short, durable written record of one specific technical decision — what we decided, why, what we gave up, and what else we considered. The problem it solves is that a decision made only in a meeting lives in whoever's memory was in that room, and memory is lossy: six months later someone asks "why do we use this vector database instead of that one," and without a written record the honest answer is "I think there was a meeting, let me ask around." The structure is deliberately simple: Context (the situation at the time), Decision (one clear sentence), Consequences (the real trade-offs, including the negative ones), and Alternatives Considered. That last section is actually the one I'd point you to first — the most common question anyone asks about a past decision isn't "what did we choose," it's "why didn't we choose the other thing," and the ADR already has that answer written down instead of making someone reconstruct it from memory, possibly after the original decision-maker has left the team.

exercises.title: Explaining build vs. buy and total cost of ownership to a confused new hire
exercises.skillTag: Build vs. Buy & Total Cost of Ownership
exercises.situation: A new engineer on the team is surprised the team decided to build a re-ranking component in-house instead of just paying for a managed API, and asks why anyone would choose to build something that already exists as a product.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We just figured building it ourselves would be cheaper, so we went with that.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It states a conclusion with no actual reasoning behind it — no real numbers, no time horizon, and no mention of the non-cost factors (team expertise, vendor risk, speed to market) that belong in a build-vs-buy decision. It leaves the new engineer with no model for how to make this kind of decision themselves next time.
exercises.professionalResponse: Build-vs-buy decisions come down to total cost of ownership over a realistic time horizon, not just the sticker price of either option. In this case, we ran the numbers over two years: building cost about $45,000 upfront plus roughly $60,000 in ongoing maintenance, versus about $131,000 if we bought the equivalent managed re-ranking API at our current request volume — building came out roughly $26,000 cheaper over that window. But cost alone isn't the whole decision. We also weighed speed to market — building took three real months we didn't ship the feature — team expertise, since we'd built a similar component before and had reasonable confidence in the estimate, and whether re-ranking quality is actually a differentiator for us or a commodity capability any adequate vendor could provide. In our case the cost advantage, our existing expertise, and genuine product differentiation all pointed the same direction, which made build the right call here — but I'd want to run this exact analysis again for the next build-vs-buy decision rather than assuming build is always cheaper, because last time I ran these numbers for a different component, buying actually won.

exercises.title: Explaining a latency budget to someone who thinks "just make it faster" is a sufficient spec
exercises.situation: A product lead tells the team the assistant "needs to just be faster" after customer complaints, with no specific number attached, and expects engineering to simply deliver on that.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Okay, we'll work on making it faster. We'll try to speed up whatever we can.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It accepts a vague target with no actual number attached, which means there's no way to know when "faster" has actually been achieved, and no way to tell which component (embedding, retrieval, generation, network) is actually responsible for the slowness. It sets the team up to "optimize" without a real target or a way to verify success.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before we start optimizing, I'd want to agree on a specific end-to-end latency target and then split it into a budget across each step in the request path — right now we don't have a number to hit, which means we can't actually tell when we're done, or which piece is the real problem. If we agree the target should be, say, 2 seconds end to end, I'd break that into a budget table: roughly 50ms for embedding the query, 100ms for vector search, 150ms for re-ranking, 1,200ms for the LLM generation itself, and 500ms for network and overhead. That turns "make it faster" into something each team can actually be held to — if vector search comes in at 300ms instead of its 100ms budget, that's now a specific, measurable problem against an agreed number, not a vague feeling that "the whole thing is slow." I'd also want real data on where today's latency is actually going before we assume which piece needs the work — it's entirely possible the slowness customers are feeling is concentrated in one specific step, not spread evenly across all of them.

exercises.title: Explaining "blameless" to a stakeholder who wants to know whose fault an incident was
exercises.situation: After a 40-minute production incident, a stakeholder outside engineering asks directly "whose fault was this" and wants the postmortem to identify who should be held responsible.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We don't really assign blame in postmortems, we just focus on fixing stuff.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It dodges the real question instead of explaining WHY blame isn't the goal, which can come across as evasive rather than principled. It also fails to clarify that blameless doesn't mean nobody made a mistake — it risks sounding like the team is avoiding accountability altogether rather than pursuing a more effective kind of it.
exercises.professionalResponse: I want to be direct about this: blameless doesn't mean we're pretending no mistake happened — an engineer did ship the change that caused the outage, and that's not in dispute. What blameless means is that the investigation's goal is understanding the systemic reasons that mistake was possible and made it all the way to production, rather than stopping at 'this person made an error.' The reason we run it this way is pragmatic, not just a nice sentiment: if we punish the individual, the lesson everyone else on the team learns is to hide mistakes and near-misses, which is strictly worse for reliability, because we lose our earliest warning signal for the next incident. In this specific case, the actual root cause — five 'whys' down — was that our test data was never re-sampled as the production knowledge base grew, so a document category added months ago was never covered by our tests. That's a process gap we can actually fix. 'Someone made a mistake' isn't fixable in any durable way; 'we have no process to keep test data representative' is.

exercises.title: Walking a VP through the 5 Whys behind a bad deploy
exercises.situation: A VP asks for a quick summary of what caused a 40-minute incident where 12% of requests failed, and seems ready to accept "a bad deploy" as the full explanation so the meeting can move on.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Yeah, it was a bad deploy. We rolled it back and we're being more careful going forward.

exercises.professionalResponse: "A bad deploy" is accurate but it's not the real root cause, and I want to walk you through why that matters. The deploy had a bug in how it handled a specific response format from the vector database. That wasn't caught because our test suite didn't cover that format — which only occurs when a document has no metadata tags, a case that's rare in our test data but common in one real document category. That category wasn't in our test data because the test data was built from a sample taken months ago, before that category existed in the knowledge base. And the reason it's stale is that we have no process that periodically re-samples test data as the knowledge base grows — it was built once and never revisited. That's five "whys" down from "a bad deploy," and it's the actual root cause: a process gap, not a one-off mistake. The fix isn't "review code more carefully" — it's a specific, owned action item: an automated monthly job that re-samples test data from the live knowledge base, which I'd want someone named and a deadline attached to before we consider this closed.

exercises.title: Diagnosing why a deflection-rate initiative isn't hitting its target
exercises.situation: Three months into a project meant to raise the AI assistant's ticket-deflection rate, the number has barely moved, and a team lead asks you to figure out why the initiative "isn't working."
exercises.beginnerResponse: I think the AI just isn't good enough yet, maybe we need a better model.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It jumps straight to a conclusion (the model itself) without actually investigating where the deflection rate is really getting lost — it could be a retrieval quality problem, a latency problem causing abandonment, a confidence-threshold routing too many answers to humans, or something else entirely. Guessing at a fix without diagnosis risks spending real engineering effort on the wrong lever.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before concluding it's the model, I'd want to actually trace where the deflection rate is getting lost, because "the AI isn't good enough" could mean several different, specific things with different fixes. First, I'd check retrieval quality directly — are the documents the assistant retrieves actually relevant, independent of how the final answer is worded? If retrieval is weak, a better model won't fix that, since it would just be generating a confident answer from bad source material. Second, I'd check our latency numbers against the budget we set — if responses are coming in slower than our target, users may be abandoning before they ever see an answer, which would show up as a deflection problem even though the root cause is pure latency, not answer quality at all. Third, I'd check how often our confidence threshold is routing answers to a human unnecessarily — if the threshold is too conservative, a correct AI answer still counts against deflection because a human handled it anyway. Only after checking these three — retrieval, latency, and threshold routing — would I actually look at whether the model's own answer quality, given good retrieval, is the real bottleneck. My guess based on similar patterns elsewhere is that it's rarely "the model," and much more often one of the first three.

exercises.skillTag: Diagnosing a Concurrency Bug Through Mentoring
exercises.situation: A junior engineer you're mentoring is stuck on a confusing bug: the RAG pipeline occasionally cites documents that were never actually retrieved, and they ask you to just tell them what's wrong.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Oh, that's probably a race condition between retrieval and prompt assembly under load. Just add a lock around that section.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It immediately hands over the diagnosis and the fix, which solves today's bug but skips the chance to teach the engineer HOW to find a concurrency bug like this themselves next time. It also jumps to a fix (a lock) before confirming the diagnosis is even correct, which risks patching the wrong thing.
exercises.professionalResponse: Rather than naming the cause right away, let me ask you a few questions first, because the answers will actually point us toward it. Does this happen under concurrent load, or can you reproduce it with a single request sent in isolation? If it only shows up under concurrent load, that's a strong hint we're looking at a race condition somewhere in how retrieval results and the prompt being assembled interact — not a logic bug that would show up every time. I'd also ask: when it happens, is the cited document from a DIFFERENT request that was in flight around the same time, or does it look unrelated to anything recent? If it's consistently a document from a near-simultaneous request, that's close to confirming a shared-state race condition, where one request's retrieval results are leaking into another request's prompt assembly because something that should be request-scoped is actually being shared. I'd want you to go reproduce it under controlled concurrent load first and confirm that hypothesis yourself, rather than me telling you it's definitely a race condition and having you just add a lock — if the hypothesis is right, you'll have learned exactly the kind of question to ask next time; if it's wrong, we'll have ruled out a specific thing cheaply instead of patching a problem that wasn't actually there.

exercises.title: Diagnosing why a tooling-free standard quietly stopped being followed
exercises.situation: Six months after the team agreed every new ADR should include an Alternatives Considered section, a new engineer notices several recent ADRs are missing it, and asks you why the standard isn't being followed anymore.
exercises.beginnerResponse: People probably just forgot, or got lazy about it. We should remind everyone again.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It blames individual forgetfulness without examining whether the standard was ever actually enforced by anything other than people's memory, and "remind everyone again" repeats the exact approach that already failed once, which means it's likely to fail again for the same reason.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before assuming people just forgot, I'd check how this standard was actually enforced in the first place — and my guess is the answer is "it wasn't, beyond people remembering to do it." If the only mechanism was a one-time announcement and everyone's good intentions, this is exactly the failure mode we should expect: a standard that depends on human memory during code review gets followed inconsistently, because reviewers are busy, new, or simply don't think to check for one specific section in a document they're reviewing for a dozen other things at once. The fact that it held for a while and then faded is actually consistent with this — early on, the standard was fresh in everyone's mind; six months later, it's one of many things a reviewer could check and isn't the thing that jumps out. Rather than reminding everyone again, which repeats the thing that already stopped working, I'd propose a CI check that fails a pull request introducing a new ADR file with no Alternatives Considered section — something that doesn't depend on anyone remembering, the same way linting doesn't depend on anyone remembering to check for a missing semicolon.

exercises.title: Diagnosing a capacity incident that was actually forecasted months earlier
exercises.situation: The team hits a real capacity ceiling and the assistant degrades under load for several hours. In the retro, someone points out a forecast from four months earlier predicted exactly this, and a director asks how this still happened anyway.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I guess the forecast just wasn't taken seriously enough at the time, we should pay more attention to forecasts going forward.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats "pay more attention" as the fix, which is just as vague and unenforceable as "review code more carefully" from a bad-deploy postmortem, and it doesn't identify the actual, specific gap between having a forecast and acting on it in time — which is the real, fixable problem.
exercises.professionalResponse: The forecast itself wasn't the failure — it was accurate, and that's actually worth confirming explicitly so we don't lose confidence in forecasting generally. The real gap is between having a forecast and translating it into a deadline anyone was actually accountable to. A forecast saying "we hit the ceiling in month 7" is not, by itself, an action item — the number that actually matters is the LEAD TIME the fix requires, and whether work started early enough given that lead time. In this case, the fix needed roughly three months of engineering work, which means it needed to start by month 4 of the forecast window to land comfortably before month 7. What I'd want to know specifically is: did anyone translate "month 7" into "start by month 4," and if so, what happened to that deadline? My guess, based on how this usually goes, is that the forecast was shared as information rather than converted into an owned, dated commitment — which is a completely different failure than "nobody read the forecast." The fix isn't "pay more attention," it's a specific process: every capacity forecast gets a required follow-up step where someone explicitly computes the required start date from the fix's lead time and assigns it an owner, not just a shared number everyone assumes someone else is tracking.

exercises.title: Defending the Weaviate vector-database decision to a skeptical engineer
exercises.situation: An engineer who joined after the vector database decision was made pushes back, arguing Pinecone would have been the obviously better, simpler choice, and asks why the team didn't just go with it.

We needed hybrid search — combining vector similarity with keyword search — for accuracy reasons, and metadata filtering for document access control, both of which Weaviate supported natively. Pinecone scored higher on operational simplicity, since it's fully managed with zero infrastructure for us to run, but scored lower on feature fit for our specific hybrid-search need and came in more expensive at our volume. Weighting those four factors for OUR situation — a team with some operational appetite, cost-sensitive at our scale, needing hybrid search specifically — Weaviate came out slightly ahead, 7.50 to 7.40. That's a close result, which I want to be honest about: a team with less operational appetite, or without the hybrid-search requirement, could reasonably weight those same factors differently and land on Pinecone instead, and that would be an equally legitimate call for THEIR situation. The full reasoning, including the exact weights and scores we used, is written up in ADR-014 if you want to see precisely how close it was and decide for yourself whether you'd have weighted it the same way.

exercises.title: Explaining the active-active multi-region decision and its real cost
exercises.situation: A finance stakeholder notices the infrastructure budget roughly doubled after a multi-region deployment and asks whether this was really necessary, given the assistant had no major outages before the change.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We needed it for reliability, outages are bad for the business, so this was worth doing.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It asserts the conclusion ("worth doing") without any real numbers behind either side of the cost-benefit comparison, which gives the finance stakeholder nothing to actually evaluate. It also fails to address the specific point raised — that there hadn't been a major outage yet — which can come across as dismissing a fair, specific question.
exercises.professionalResponse: That's a fair question, and I want to address the specific point directly: we hadn't had a major outage, which is actually exactly when this kind of investment needs to be made — before the incident, not after. At single-region, we were running at about 99.9% uptime, which sounds solid but works out to roughly 525 minutes of downtime a year — nearly 9 hours. Once we became customer-facing rather than just an internal tool, an outage of that scale means real revenue and trust impact, not just an internal inconvenience. Moving to active-active multi-region, assuming the two regions fail independently, brings that down to roughly 99.9999% uptime — about half a minute a year. The infrastructure cost roughly doubled for this specific component, which I'd weigh against the cost of even one multi-hour customer-facing outage in lost trust and potential support costs — a cost that's harder to put a precise number on but is real. I'd also flag honestly that the math I just gave assumes the two regions fail independently, and we did real work auditing for shared dependencies — the same model API account, the same auth service — that could silently break that assumption; that audit work was part of the cost too, and it's the reason this redundancy actually holds up rather than just looking good on paper.

exercises.title: Explaining the staged static-threshold-then-learned-classifier decision
exercises.situation: A data science lead asks why the team chose a simple static confidence threshold for routing low-confidence answers to humans instead of just building a proper machine-learning classifier from the start.
exercises.beginnerResponse: A learned classifier seemed like more work than we needed right now, so we just went with something simpler.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It frames the decision as avoiding effort rather than as a reasoned response to a specific, real constraint, which makes it sound like corner-cutting rather than a deliberate architecture choice. It also misses the chance to explain that the simpler option was chosen specifically because it sets up the better option for later, rather than being a dead end.
exercises.professionalResponse: It wasn't about avoiding work — a learned classifier is genuinely the more accurate approach in principle, and I'd want to build toward it. The specific constraint was data: training or validating a classifier reliably requires a real labeled dataset of "was this answer actually correct," and we don't have that at volume yet. Starting with a static threshold, tuned against a small manually-labeled sample, gets us shipping quickly without pretending we have data we don't have. But the more important point is that this isn't a dead end — the static-threshold period itself generates exactly the labeled outcome data a future classifier would need to be trained and validated properly. So the sequencing is deliberate: static threshold now, specifically because it's also the preparation step for the learned classifier later, once we've accumulated real data. I wrote this reasoning into an ADR, including the honest trade-off that a fixed cutoff won't generalize as well across different question types as a learned model eventually would — we're accepting that imprecision now in exchange for shipping sooner and building the exact dataset we'd need to do better later.

exercises.professionalResponse: I want to be specific about why this isn't just general cleanup — it's a real dependency for the feature you asked for. exercises.situation: A VP of Customer Support asks directly whether the AI assistant could ever show one customer's support ticket information to a different customer, after hearing about a data-leakage incident at another company.

exercises.professionalResponse: I want to give you something more specific than reassurance, because that question deserves a real answer. Every retrieval query is scoped by customer ID at the database level, before anything reaches the AI model — so a cross-customer leak would require that specific isolation check to fail, not just an unlucky answer or a confused model. We test this isolation boundary directly as part of our deployment checks, and it's been part of every release for the past year with zero violations found. I'd estimate the likelihood as very low specifically because it depends on a single, well-tested mechanism rather than the model's own judgment — which is different from, say, a hallucination risk, where the mechanism itself is inherently probabilistic. If it did fail, the impact would be serious — a real privacy violation, not just a wrong answer — which is why this specific check gets tested on every release rather than periodically. The ask I'd have for you: if we're ever adding a new data source or a new retrieval path, I'd want this isolation boundary explicitly re-verified as part of that rollout, not assumed to carry over automatically.

exercises.title: Explaining why a great-looking eval result deserves skepticism before a launch decision
exercises.skillTag: Communicating Evaluation Result Uncertainty to Leadership
exercises.situation: Leadership is excited about a new prompt variant that scored dramatically better on an internal evaluation set and wants to greenlight an immediate full rollout, asking you to confirm it's ready to ship.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The eval numbers look great, I think we're good to ship it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It takes one good-looking result at face value without asking the obvious follow-up question a dramatically better score deserves — was this actually tested on genuinely new, unseen scenarios, or could the improvement be an artifact of how it was tuned against this specific eval set. Recommending a full rollout on that basis risks shipping something that looks great in testing and underperforms in the real, more varied traffic it'll actually face.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before recommending a full rollout, I want to ask one specific question, because a dramatically better eval score is exactly the kind of result that deserves real scrutiny rather than immediate excitement: was this prompt variant tuned and selected using the SAME eval set it's now being scored against, or was it validated on a separate, held-out set it never touched during development? If it was tuned against this exact eval set — trying many variants and picking the best-scoring one — then this score is likely to be somewhat inflated, because the variant was selected partly for fitting this specific set's particular quirks, not just for being genuinely better in general. That's not a reason to assume the result is fake, but it is a reason to validate it differently before a full rollout: I'd recommend a staged rollout to a small percentage of real traffic first, measuring the SAME metrics on genuinely new, unseen interactions, before committing to 100%. If the improvement holds up on real traffic the variant never saw during tuning, that's much stronger evidence than the original eval score alone, however good that score looked.

exercises.situation: Leadership is frustrated that the hybrid-search feature they prioritized hasn't launched yet, and asks directly why engineering isn't just focused on shipping it as fast as possible.

exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: "Some other stuff" gives leadership no way to evaluate whether the delay is justified or just poor prioritization, and it doesn't connect the delay back to the business goal leadership actually cares about. exercises.professionalResponse: I want to connect this directly back to the goal you set — reducing support costs 20% through higher AI deflection — because the sequencing decision was made specifically to serve that goal, not to delay your feature for its own sake. Hybrid search depends on a shared piece of code that's currently duplicated five times across the system; building hybrid search on top of that as-is would mean implementing it five separate times, which is slower overall and creates an ongoing maintenance cost every time that logic changes afterward. We ran the numbers: the one-week refactor pays for itself in under two years just from reduced maintenance cost, before even counting that it makes the hybrid-search work itself faster and less error-prone. So the actual choice wasn't "refactor vs. your feature" — it was "spend one week now to make your feature land faster and more reliably, or spend longer building it five times over and dealing with the maintenance cost indefinitely afterward." The refactor is done as of this week, and hybrid search is now the next item up, with a real timeline I can share, rather than an open-ended "soon."

exercises.situation: A capacity-tier migration completed on schedule, and a stakeholder asks whether the capacity problem is now fully resolved, seemingly expecting a quick yes.

exercises.professionalResponse: The migration completing is a milestone, but I want to distinguish that from actually confirming the capacity problem is resolved — those aren't automatically the same thing. exercises.skillTag: Explaining a Gap Between Calculated and Observed Availability
exercises.situation: Several months after a multi-region deployment calculated at 99.9999% theoretical uptime, an actual regional outage took down both regions at once, and a stakeholder asks how the math could have been so wrong.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I guess the calculation was just too optimistic, these things happen sometimes.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats the gap between the calculated number and what actually happened as an unexplainable surprise rather than investigating the SPECIFIC reason the independence assumption behind the math broke down. It also doesn't propose any concrete fix, which means the same gap is likely to recur.
exercises.professionalResponse: The math wasn't wrong in general — it was correct under a specific assumption that turned out not to hold in this case, and I want to be precise about which one, because that's what actually needs fixing. The 99.9999% figure assumed the two regions would fail independently. What actually happened was both regions went down together because they shared a single upstream dependency — in this case, both regions used the same model API account, and that account hit a provider-side issue that affected every region tied to it simultaneously. That's a textbook shared dependency breaking the independence assumption the whole calculation rested on — the redundancy was real for infrastructure-level failures like a data center outage, but it was never actually independent with respect to THIS specific failure mode. The fix isn't to distrust the math generally, it's to specifically audit for and eliminate this category of shared dependency — in this case, setting up a genuinely separate model-provider account for the second region, so a provider-account-level issue doesn't take down both regions at once the way this one did.

exercises.professionalResponse: That's worth actually checking against real data rather than relying on an impression, so let me walk through it. The original projection was that the refactor's one-engineer-week cost would break even in under two years, based on an estimated carrying cost of a few thousand dollars a year in extra engineering time per change. Looking at our actual change history since the refactor, the frequency of changes to this code turned out to be roughly what we estimated, and — more importantly — each change is now measurably faster, based on time-tracking data from recent pull requests touching this code versus pull requests from before the refactor. Putting those real numbers together, the refactor looks to have actually broken even around month 14, a bit earlier than the original 2-year projection, mostly because this code changed slightly more often than originally estimated. So the honest answer is yes, it was worth it, and I can show you the actual data rather than just an impression that the code "feels cleaner" — though I'd also flag that our original estimate was directionally right but not exactly precise, which is useful to know for how much confidence to put in similar estimates going forward.

exercises.title: Explaining why an architecture review ended without a decision, and what changes next time
exercises.skillTag: Validating and Improving a Failed Review Process
exercises.situation: An architecture review you ran ended with "lots to think about, let's reconvene" and no actual decision, and your own manager asks you afterward what happened and what you'd do differently.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It just didn't really come to a conclusion, I think we needed more time to think it through.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats the lack of a decision as simply needing more time, without diagnosing the actual, specific reason the review stalled — which is the real, useful information a manager would want. It also offers no concrete change for next time, which means the same failure mode is likely to repeat in the next review.
exercises.professionalResponse: I want to be honest about this rather than chalk it up to needing more time, because I think I can point to the specific reason it stalled. Looking back at the design doc, it presented only one option with no real alternatives section — which meant when a reviewer raised a partial objection, they had no way to say "I like this but I'm worried about X" without it sounding like a full rejection, so the room defaulted to deferring instead of deciding. That's a known failure pattern, not just bad luck: a design doc with no visible alternatives forces an all-or-nothing choice, and most people are reluctant to force a full rejection over a partial concern. What I'd do differently next time is make sure the document includes at least one real alternative before the review, specifically so a reviewer with a partial objection has a path to say "I prefer this over the alternative, but address this one thing" instead of being stuck between full approval and full rejection. I'd also explicitly state the decision being asked for at the start of the meeting, rather than framing it as an open discussion, since that framing invites exactly the kind of open-ended conversation that has no natural stopping point.
